Full layouts of thread state, address-space and page descriptors beyond the members referenced by these fragments.
Internals of asynchronous fault reporting, tag synchronization on mapping changes and tag-check override handling.
Complete hypervisor shared-record layout, hypercall numbers and error-code definitions beyond success and revision checks.
Full instruction encoding, temporary-mapping and cache-maintenance contracts for live text patching.

findings.text: Page comparison reports byte equality across a full page, but treats identical bytes as distinct when tagging is active on either input and the inputs reside at different addresses, preventing reuse of a tagged page as an untagged equivalent.

Kernel tag checking at privileged level offers separate activation operations for synchronous, asynchronous, asymmetric and store-only checking, each applying its mode to the privileged control register and ordering the change before later execution.

Privileged checking starts in synchronous operation; the first processor selecting asynchronous or asymmetric operation promotes a system-wide indicator exactly once, asymmetric operation requires a dedicated capability with fallback to synchronous operation when absent, and store-only filtering is independent and rejected when its capability is absent.

The privileged fault status is examined for a single fault indicator; when present the status is cleared without an extra ordering operation and an asynchronous tag fault report is requested, otherwise no action occurs.

User checking for a thread resolves requested modes against a per-processor preferred mode, using the preferred value when it overlaps the request and the request otherwise, with asymmetric preferred over asynchronous over synchronous and store-only handled orthogonally; the caller must hold preemption disabled on the target processor and apply the cached control value later in the same disabled region.

Per-thread user tag control translates between user-visible inclusion and fault-mode requests and an internal exclusion and mode representation, inverting the tag mask, mapping each fault-mode request bit, implying asymmetric mode when both synchronous and asynchronous are requested on capable systems, and refreshing live registers immediately when the target is the current thread.

New user threads clear any pending asynchronous fault indicator and reset their tag control when tagging is supported; context switch refreshes the next thread user controls and tag-generation state, ensures tag-check override is disabled for the incoming thread, and checks privileged fault status when system-wide asynchronous operation is active; suspend entry performs a similar ordered fault-status check.

A tracer can read or write tags of another task through a single vector describing a local buffer and length, with the target address aligned down to tag granularity; the operation requires tagging support, a live address space and ptracer permission, validates the tracer buffer, and distinguishes read from write by request type.

Remote tag transfer proceeds page by page, requiring each target mapping to carry the tag-enabled attribute, warning when a nonzero page lacks expected tagging state, limiting each step to the remainder of the current page expressed in tag units, marking written pages dirty, and reporting the number of tags moved through the vector length with distinct errors for tracee versus tracer access failures.

Low-level helpers move a requested number of tags between tagged memory accessed at tag granularity and a bytewise user buffer, tolerating faults on the user side and returning how many tags were actually transferred, with zero length completing immediately.

Each processor exposes a preferred user fault-mode attribute supporting asynchronous, synchronous and, where capable, asymmetric values, defaulting to asynchronous at registration, rejecting unknown text, and updating per-processor storage under device serialization.

Per-processor stolen-time state consists of a single read-copy-update protected pointer to a hypervisor-shared stolen-time record, initially empty and populated only after successful discovery and mapping.

Stolen-time support is discovered through feature queries, then each online processor requests its shared record address, maps it writably cached, validates that revision and attribute fields are zero, and publishes the pointer; offline processing clears the pointer, waits for readers, and releases the mapping, with failures reported without publishing.

Stolen-time queries read the per-processor shared record under read-side protection and return its little-endian counter, returning zero when the processor has no published record yet, including when queried before its online notification.

Paravirt time initialization probes for stolen-time availability, installs per-processor online and offline handlers, redirects the steal-clock indirection to the hypervisor-backed reader, enables accounting keys with request-queue accounting controlled by a boot option defaulting to enabled, and logs successful use.

Live text updates serialize on a dedicated raw spinlock with interrupts saved, rewrite the target in page-bounded chunks through a temporary writable mapping that is unmapped after each chunk, and flush the instruction cache over the whole range after releasing the lock.
Instruction memory can be overwritten from a source buffer or filled with a repeated instruction word, both rejecting unaligned destinations without side effects.
Coordinated multi-address patching uses a descriptor holding parallel arrays of destination addresses and replacement words with a count, plus a shared arrival counter used to elect a single writer.

Multi-processor text patching runs a callback on every online processor where the last arrival performs all word replacements without cross-processor synchronization and then releases the others, while early arrivals spin until released and then order execution before returning; empty or negative counts are rejected without action.

Raw configuration reads and writes locate the referenced bus and delegate to its operations, reporting device-not-found when the bus is absent; node lookup for a bus delegates to its generic device node.

User callchain collection skips guest state entirely, otherwise records the current program counter and walks frame pointers, selecting a 64-bit or 32-bit compatibility walker based on processor mode and stopping when the consumer declines further entries.

User frame unwinding validates each frame address for accessibility and alignment, copies the frame atomically with faults disabled, strips pointer authentication from return addresses in 64-bit mode, and requires frame pointers to strictly ascend toward higher addresses, terminating on any violation or copy failure.
Remote tag access holds the target address space read lock in killable form for the whole page loop and always releases it before returning, including on early permission, mapping, or buffer errors.

Stolen-time readers use read-side critical sections around pointer dereference and counter sampling, writers publish with assignment ordering, and teardown replaces the pointer under full ordering, waits for a grace period, then unmaps.
Live updates to the current thread tag control disable preemption across cache update, generation-state update, and register application to keep the processor and thread consistent.
Preferred-mode stores serialize per-device updates with device locking around the per-processor assignment.
User stack unwinding disables page faults only around the atomic frame copy and re-enables immediately after, after a prior accessibility check over the full frame.

Privileged and user control changes require an instruction barrier after the write, fault-status checks on switch and suspend rely on data and instruction barriers to synchronize indirect status writes, and thread initialization orders fault clearing with a data barrier.
Merging pages with identical bytes but differing tagged state risks later tag alteration of the shared page through mapping tag synchronization, so such pages must be reported as distinct.
Entering synchronous kernel mode while system-wide asynchronous or asymmetric operation is already active indicates an unexpected global mode mix and is flagged once without changing behavior.

User control application to the privileged register masks to user-writable bits while preserving the in-kernel authentication enable, followed by an ordering barrier needed for kernel access routines when user fault control changes.

User tag control uses distinct request bits for asynchronous checking, synchronous checking and store-only filtering plus a shifted tag-inclusion field, mirrored by internal mode bits and a shifted exclusion field with random-generation selection.

Tag transfer distinguishes a poke request selecting writable access from other requests selecting read-only access, aligns targets down to tag granularity, and moves data in tag-sized steps with bytewise tracer progress.
The preferred-mode attribute uses three textual values for asynchronous, synchronous and asymmetric operation with a distinct placeholder for unexpected stored values, and rejects unsupported text.

Stolen-time negotiation uses architecture feature and time-feature hypercalls with success and not-supported outcomes, a stolen-time request identifier, and requires zero revision and attributes in the shared record.
An early boot fixup converts a single branch into a no-operation when hardware-tagged sanitizer operation is enabled, asserting that exactly one instruction is patched.
Tag-generation exclusion is programmed from the thread control value with random selection enabled, but skipped entirely when hardware-tagged sanitizer operation manages generation state.

Compatibility-mode unwinding adjusts for a smaller frame layout and pointer conversion when validating progress and computing the next frame, while sharing accessibility, atomic copy and termination rules with 64-bit unwinding.

Requesting asymmetric operation without its capability falls back to synchronous checking, and requesting store-only filtering without its capability fails without side effects while absence of tagging support makes control queries report zero.
Paravirt log output uses a fixed textual prefix identifying the subsystem.
